correctness.rationale: Theorem 1.1 of arXiv:2608.04392v1 fixes the global maximizer and stationarity. Direct algebra verifies its nine unit vertices, fourteen strict triangular supporting facets, 21 edges, signed determinant volume 3h and exact stationary tangent gradients. The full 18-dimensional constrained Hessian is reconstructed from trilinear determinants and the sphere second fundamental form. The three rotation columns have exactly diagonal Gram \(W^{\mathsf T}W=\operatorname{diag}(g,g,k)\) and are null by rotation invariance at the critical point. The stand-alone integer interval checker rigorously proves \(-\mathcal H+P-(39/100)I\) positive definite via all 18 positive LDL pivots (each >0.05575). Uniform Taylor expansion on the compact rotation orbit proves the claimed local deficit constant 0.1. The checker was replayed from the actual included path and printed VERIFY_OK; finite residuals never substitute for analytic identities.

originality.rationale: Full primary text of Hoehner–Ledford, arXiv:2608.04392v1, supplies only the configuration/global bound and a Hessian of an unrelated two-variable star-inequality auxiliary function. No transverse constrained 18-by-18 spectral certificate or uniform quadratic near-orbit volume deficit is supplied. Targeted literature and mathematical-record comparisons did not identify an equivalent claim; unindexed prior local computations remain possible.
residual_risks: An unindexed independent second-variation computation, especially in polyhedral numerical optimization, might express the same result without nine-vertex or Hessian terminology.
Full text of some older cited works was not available/read; the specifically relevant contemporary primary source was materially inspected in full-text form.
The interval-certified 0.39 gap is not claimed optimal; neither a global stability radius nor a global inequality follows.

value.rationale: The new full normal-spectrum estimate proves Morse–Bott nondegeneracy and a quantitative quadratic volume deficit for all 15 nonrotational deformation modes of the newly solved nine-point extremal problem. Unlike uniqueness alone, it distinguishes quadratic from potentially quartic flatness and provides a reproducible robust curvature bound for near-optimal configurations. This is a geometrically natural local stability theorem, not an arbitrary subfamily or a numerical table recomputation.
